title: Lost for three days (Luke 2:41–52)
hook: twelve-year-old Jesus stays in the Temple and asks why they didn't know he'd be in his Father's house

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epiphany, strangers from the east, and then a family running for Egypt. The holy family were refugees. Week five begins: the beginning.
screen: `THE HOLY FAMILY WERE REFUGEES.` → `WEEK FIVE: THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: A parent turns around in a crowded market, and the child isn't there. Now stretch that moment to three days. Every year, Luke says, Mary and Joseph walked to Jerusalem for the Passover in a big crowd of relatives and neighbors. The year Jesus is twelve, they start home assuming he's somewhere in the caravan with the cousins. A whole day's walk later, they realize he isn't. They turn back and search Jerusalem. One day. Two. Three.
screen: `YOU TURN AROUND. HE'S GONE.` → `A DAY'S WALK BEFORE THEY NOTICE.` → `ONE DAY. TWO. THREE.`

segments.voice: They find him, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the scholars of the law. A twelve-year-old from a village sits among them, and Luke says everyone was astonished at how he understood and how he answered. Mary says what a frightened parent says: "Son, why hast thou done so to us? behold thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." Sorrowing: three days of it. His answer is the first thing Jesus says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that you sought me? did you not know, that I must be about my father's business?" In Luke's Greek the phrase is short and open: in the things of my Father. Older English Bibles say business; some newer ones say house. Both are possible. Either way: I'm where I belong. Luke admits they didn't understand him, not even Mary. He goes home with them and obeys them, and Mary keeps all these things in her heart, the same words Luke used after the shepherds. Catholics hold this story in two places at once. It's the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the finding in the Temple: a joy. And it's one of the seven sorrows of Mary. Notice where they found him. Not playing, not lost and crying. Asking questions. It's his first scene past babyhood, and in it, questions aren't the opposite of faith.
screen: `SITTING AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `THY FATHER AND I HAVE SOUGHT THEE.` · `IN THE THINGS OF MY FATHER.` · `A JOY AND A SORROW.` · then, large: `THEY FOUND HIM ASKING QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you once lost: for a few minutes in a crowd, for years to a falling-out, or for good. Remember what the searching felt like, without hurrying past it. If they were found, remember that moment too; if not, hold them gently, and if you pray, bring them to God.
Doctors. In Luke's story, the teachers of the law in the Temple, where the boy sat listening and asking.
Your line: they found him asking questions. Not lost, not crying: asking. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics meditate on this story as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the Finding in the Temple, and as one of the Seven Sorrows of Mary; it is read on the feast of the Holy Family.

original.note: Greek: in the things of my Father. it can mean his house or his business; translations differ.

what a scholar hears: en tois tou patros mou, ambiguous between house and affairs; three days foreshadowing the three days before Easter.
